sample_unit: datasets (six chest X-ray datasets plus dermatology and ophthalmology datasets)

links.outcome: Fairness gaps after algorithmic shortcut correction, in-distribution versus external test sets
links.effect: Algorithmic correction closed fairness gaps in the original data distribution ('locally optimal'), but this did not hold in new test settings; models with less demographic encoding were often more fair externally.
links.quote: Although correcting shortcuts algorithmically effectively addresses fairness gaps to create 'locally optimal' models within the original data distribution, this optimality is not true in new test settings.

links.outcome: Fairness of imaging AI in external test environments versus in-distribution evaluation
links.effect: In-distribution fairness did not carry over to new test settings; models with less demographic encoding were often most 'globally optimal', with better fairness in new test environments.
links.quote: Surprisingly, we found that models with less encoding of demographic attributes are often most 'globally optimal', exhibiting better fairness during model evaluation in new test environments.

unlisted_practices: Select models for deployment based on reduced encoding of demographic attributes to maintain fairness across sites

screen.reason: Evaluates fairness discrepancies and algorithmic demographic shortcut correction across multiple benchmark datasets, but focuses on model-level algorithmic mitigation and generalization rather than testing an organizational deployment safeguard.
